signals.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks | Artificial Intelligence
signals.excerpt:
When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund.

We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop.

With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints.

There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use.

...

## A more capable managed harness

Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults:

- A current recommended model. When you omit the model, Harness uses a recommended default model that evolves as new models are released, always keeping your harnesses up to date. Explicit harness-level and per-invocation model configurations continue to take precedence.
- Task-oriented instructions. The managed system prompt encourages the agent to gather relevant context, use appropriate tools, continue until the task is resolved, adapt to failures or denied actions, and verify its work before reporting completion. The default system prompt improves over time to support the latest harness behavior.
- Automatic prompt caching. For supported models using Converse on Amazon Bedrock, Harness caches the system prompt, tool definitions, and conversation history. Repeated calls with the same prompt and tool surface can use lower-priced cache-read tokens, reducing input processing latency and cost.
- Proactive context management. By default, Harness summarizes older conversation turns while retaining recent context once the context window reaches a configurable threshold. Keeping the context lean this way helps Harness run at about 34% lower token cost than other leading harnesses.
- Context offloading. Large tool results can be moved out of the immediate model context. The agent receives a preview and can retrieve the complete result when needed, reducing repeated context usage without losing access to the data.
- Planning across invocations. The `todo_write` tool maintains a structured task plan that can be restored in later invocations within the same session, including after conversation summarization.
- Focused delegation. The `subagent` tool delegates a self-contained task to a fresh worker and returns the result to the parent agent. The worker is internal to the invocation, not a separately managed harness resource, and shares invocation limits and your tool-call lifecycle hooks.
- Web retrieval. The `web_fetch` tool retrieves content from a specified webpage to give your harness up-to-date external context.
- Granular filesystem access. With separate `read`, `write`, and `edit` tools, you can grant only the granular filesystem capabilities an agent needs.

signals.title: Cerebras Launches Disaggregated Inference
signals.excerpt:
Nov 17 2026

# Cerebras launches disaggregated inference

We’ve deployed Cerebras Wafer Scale Engines with GPUs to deliver lightning-fast tokens at scale

The world is hungry for ultrafast tokens. In 2026, Cerebras saw an insatiable demand for fast inference, both on our inference cloud and via our partners. To meet demand, we began developing disaggregated inference: GPUs handle prompt processing (prefill) and Cerebras systems handle output generation (decode).

This solution is now in production and delivers five times more tokens per megawatt at the same ultrafast Cerebras speeds.

We can now serve more ultrafast tokens via Cerebras Inference Cloud to meet market demand. Infrastructure partners can also leverage the Cerebras disaggregated solution to achieve more ultrafast tokens in their own datacenters.

Alongside our recently announced CS-4, our dramatically scaled manufacturing, and our planned 700MW of data center capacity, disaggregated inference will enable Cerebras and partners to serve many more ultrafast tokens in 2027 and beyond.

...

### Why Cerebras is advantaged for decode

An inference request has two main stages. Prompt processing, known as prefill, processes the input and produces intermediate model state. Response generation, known as decode, uses that state to generate output tokens. There are many ways to split the inference workload, including draft–target and attention–FFN among others, but separating prefill from decode is uniquely advantageous when the goal is highly interactive inference.

Decode is autoregressive. That means the model generates one token at a time, using each generated token as an input to generate the next. Each step means reading model data from memory again, so memory bandwidth matters a lot. In the ultrafast inference domain, SRAM-centric chips have an advantage because they can keep that data on-chip and read it much more quickly. Cerebras takes this to wafer scale, with tens of gigabytes of SRAM and tens of petabytes per second of memory bandwidth on a single chip—350× the SRAM capacity and 5,400× the memory bandwidth of a typical GB300 GPU. This allows the Cerebras System to fit more concurrent requests and model layers directly on the chip, enabling the CS-3, CS-4, and CS-5 to achieve ultrafast speeds at an attractive throughput.

### Cerebras disaggregated inference production results

Pairing Cerebras systems, which are optimized for ultrafast decode, with accelerators well-suited to the compute needs of prefill, such as AMD Instinct GPUs, allows the delivery of an immense amount of ultrafast inference at scale. In a production deployment on the Cerebras Inference Cloud, AMD Instinct GPUs process prompts, and Cerebras CS-3 systems generate responses. Moving prompt processing to GPUs allows Cerebras systems to devote their serving capacity to response generation. In our measured production deployment, this combination delivered 5X the throughput per megawatt of a CS-3-only configuration, with no loss in token generation speed.

Source: November 14th shared GPT-OSS-120B endpoint via the Cerebras Inference Cloud throughput per megawatt before and after enabling disaggregated inference, normalized to the aggregated inference baseline (1×). 

We plan to deploy disaggregated inference broadly across hundreds of megawatts in the Cerebras Inference Cloud and in partner deployments by the end of 2027. Our aim is to increase the ultrafast inference capacity available for our customers.

signals.excerpt:
November 18, 2026 ・ 5 min read

Today, we’re launching the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration, available now as the open-source strands-mongodb Python package. Strands, built and maintained by AWS, is an open-source framework for building AI agents. With this integration, MongoDB becomes the single data platform behind your Strands agents, providing:

- Session persistence, so agents can resume conversations and complex tasks after a restart or on a different instance.
- Long-term memory for facts and lessons that carry across conversations.
- Vector search to retrieve relevant past interactions by meaning.

Strands’ MemoryManager decides what to remember and when to recall it, while MongoDB handles where it’s stored and how it’s retrieved, so there’s no custom memory code to build or maintain. And because your operational data already lives in MongoDB, agents can use Atlas Vector Search to ground their answers in it, with no copy synced to a separate vector database.

## What is the Strands Harness SDK?

The Strands Harness SDK helps developers build AI agents. It manages the agent loop while giving developers control over how agents execute tasks and maintain context. Support for memory, sessions, and hooks lets developers shape agent behavior and connect agents to their application’s data and persistence layer. It provides pluggable storage and memory interfaces, with built-in backends for local files and Amazon S3. Integrations like this one let you swap in another backing service without rewriting your agent’s core logic.

signals.title: NVIDIA Releases Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Experimental Checkpoint :: Neural Wire
signals.excerpt:
### Experimental Mixed-Precision Checkpoint Released for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next

NVIDIA has released an experimental mixed-precision Quantization-Aware Deployment (QAD) checkpoint for the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model. According to the model card documentation, the release, identified as `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4-QAD`, is intended for testing purposes and utilizes mixed-precision techniques.

The release has prompted technical discussion within developer communities, specifically on Reddit, regarding its efficiency compared to existing quantized versions of the model.

### Technical Comparisons and Performance Observations

Early assessments from independent developers suggest that the experimental checkpoint may face competition from existing optimized versions. Specifically, users on Reddit have noted that the `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local` variant appears to offer superior performance characteristics for certain hardware configurations.

Technical observations shared by community members highlight several key differences in quantization strategies:

- Memory Efficiency: The `FP4-Local` version reportedly utilizes NVFP4 and MXFP8 more broadly, alongside CSF-compressed scaling factors. These optimizations are estimated to reduce the model size by approximately 3GB.
- Hardware Throughput: On professional-grade hardware, such as the RTX PRO 6000, users have reported that the `FP4-Local` variant allows for a token pool of approximately 1 million tokens, which is double the capacity of the ~130GB NVFP4 models. Additionally, the `FP4-Local` version is noted for providing higher throughput per request.
- Quantization Methods: While the experimental checkpoint uses mixed-precision QAD, other versions, such as those released by RadixArk, utilize a method where only the experts are quantized to NVFP4, borrowing FP8 PLE parameters from the original Qwen FP8 checkpoint.

Some developers have expressed skepticism regarding the utility of the new experimental checkpoint, noting that it appears significantly larger and slower than the `FP4-Local` alternative without providing immediate, obvious gains in performance or efficiency.

Today we're launching Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API, available in preview in the Interactions API.

When an agent connects to dozens or even hundreds of tools, sending every full parameter schema on every request adds up fast. It inflates input token counts, adds latency, and lowers tool-selection accuracy as the candidate list grows. Tool Retrieval lets your agent keep its full tool library on standby and load parameter schemas only when the current task needs them.

## How it works

To turn on Tool Retrieval, add a `tool_search` tool to your request and set `defer_loading: true` on the tools you want to hold back. The model still sees the name and description of every deferred tool, so it knows what's available, but the parameter schemas stay out of context. When the model needs a tool, it asks for it by name, the API loads the full schema, and the model calls the function, all inside the same request.

signals.title: The evolution of GraphRAG: Advancing systems and evaluation together - Microsoft Research
signals.excerpt:
### At a glance

- GraphRAG Zero gives AI agents the connected context they need to reason, make decisions, and act, built and updated continuously at interactive speed. 
- It’s the result of years of research, turning graph-based retrieval from an experimental technique into a deployable system built for real-world applications and agents.
- GraphRAG is now available as an option in Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search), so customers and developers can use graph-guided retrieval at scale.
- Knowledge graphs are built on Microsoft Research’s GraphRAG research, bringing commercial, graph-guided retrieval to Foundry IQ (opens in new tab) and GitHub’s Repo Mind Light, supporting applications from scientific discovery to repository understanding.
- From dataset-wide sensemaking to interactive retrieval, GraphRAG’s evolution has reduced cost and latency while preserving access to relevant, representative evidence.
- The original paper now has 3.9k citations since April 2024 and the open-source repo (opens in new tab) has over 36k GitHub stars. It has spawned a wide range of follow-on research and software.

GraphRAG Zero is designed to solve one of the fundamental challenges preventing AI agents from reaching their full potential — giving them the context they need to reason, make decisions, and act intelligently. 

AI agents need more than text excerpts that merely match the words in a prompt. To answer complex queries and understand connections across different kinds of information, they need retrieval that captures the structure within the data. This becomes increasingly important as AI generates more information than people can review. GraphRAG provides that structure, while its latest version, GraphRAG Zero, makes retrieval fast and affordable enough to build and update continuously.

...

When we shared our GraphRAG research and open-source library (opens in new tab) in 2024, we introduced a way to ask questions that conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) struggled to answer. Instead of finding only individual facts or passages, people could ask about themes, patterns, and implications across an entire collection of documents.

The impact extended beyond adoption of our library. GraphRAG helped broaden the field’s focus from finding relevant passages to organizing connected evidence for reasoning across a dataset. Today, new research approaches and open-source implementations explore this design space, while industry tooling makes graph-based retrieval available to application developers. GraphRAG has also been featured in Gartner’s Hype Cycle for Generative AI (opens in new tab).

...

The result has been two connected lines of research: successive generations of GraphRAG, and an evolving evaluation framework, BenchmarkQED (opens in new tab). Together, they have now brought a new and lightweight version of GraphRAG – GraphRAG Zero – into products. Compared to the original GraphRAG, this version eliminates LLM calls at index time and can be configured to retrieve relevant context without LLM calls at query time either, delivering sub-second retrieval latency powered entirely by the geometry of text embeddings.

GraphRAG Zero is now available as an option within Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search) (opens in new tab), bringing graph-guided retrieval to applications that need relevant, representative evidence at interactive speeds. Microsoft Discovery is also committing to adopt GraphRAG Zero through Foundry IQ to support scientific research. 

GitHub Next’s Repo Mind Light (opens in new tab), a tool for repository understanding, ships with GraphRAG Zero and is available as a public container integrated with GitHub Agentic Workflows (opens in new tab). It combines GraphRAG Zero retrieval over issues and pull requests with live retrieval of code and documentation, giving people and coding agents context for questions about architecture, ownership, and the reasoning behind earlier decisions.

...

Context that is affordable to build and keep current also supports checking what agents produce. VeriTrail works across RAG systems with source data and context-driven outputs, detecting hallucinations and tracing where unsupported content was introduced and how faithful content derives from the source.

...

### Evaluating GraphRAG Zero: From answers to evidence

LazyGraphRAG reduced preparation costs by moving language-model work to query time. The resulting delay before answer generation, however, remained a constraint for interactive applications. GraphRAG Zero addresses this with an embedding-derived graph that assembles relevant, representative context. In its real-time configuration, generative-model processing is reserved for the final response. The research evaluation below helps explain the approach behind today’s release; these results are not measurements of the Foundry IQ service.

...

In the GraphRAG Zero study, we applied these measures to podcast transcripts and news articles using 200 synthetic questions, split equally between multi-hop and global queries. At a 50-chunk retrieval budget, global answer assertion coverage increased from 53.4 percent with vector RAG to 57.4 percent with GraphRAG Zero. Both used the same embedding model and answer generator, producing one response per query. GraphRAG Zero prepared the answer context in 0.93 seconds on average, including query embedding and excluding answer generation.

Sub-second retrieval changes the experience of asking a question. LazyGraphRAG and deep-research-style workflows can spend a minute or more gathering and analyzing evidence; here, answer generation can begin almost immediately. That is the practical meaning of “Zero”: retrieval at the pace of an interactive conversation.

GraphRAG Zero achieved higher cluster recall and topical fidelity, while vector RAG retained higher chunk precision. More representative evidence supported more complete global answers, showing why the relevant-chunk fraction alone was insufficient to guide development.

Optional reasoning extensions improve global answer coverage with additional model processing. GraphRAG Zero is already widely used across Microsoft. Its release through Foundry IQ and Repo Mind Light brings the same research direction to additional application and agent workflows, where retrieval quality must be considered alongside latency, cost, and ease of use.

signals.title: Co-Designing Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Inference | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Agentic workloads, long documents, and large codebases are pushing context lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds of thousands. At those lengths, attention becomes the most expensive part of a transformer layer. Dense attention scores every query against every key, so its cost per query grows with the context length N, and at 128K tokens it can take most of the prefill time in a layer.

The model-level solution is sparse attention, a transformer technique in which each query attends to only a small subset of the context, chosen per query, instead of all of it. This cuts both the compute and the memory traffic of attention on long context.

This post is a practical primer for model developers designing sparse attention that runs well on NVIDIA GPUs. It focuses on model-level sparse attention, where sparsity is trained into the model, rather than drop-in methods applied after training such as BLASST, MInference, or Quest. A production FP8 kernel is used to sweep the indexer’s design knobs (query heads, key heads, head dimension, compression ratio, and speculative-decoding depth), measure how Top-k cost scales, and compare token-level with block-level core attention.

Each section explains what the hardware rewards and why, and ends with a guideline you can apply to your own design. This post follows the same co-design approach as the earlier posts on dense attention and hardware-friendly LLM design.

signals.title: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency | RadixArk Blog
signals.excerpt:
November 18, 2026

# DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

We are releasing BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints for everyone to try and build on. In this post, we explain how carefully designed tasks and efficient infrastructure made these gains possible on a limited compute budget.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above 1. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, a notoriously hard long-horizon benchmark. Our magic lies in the following three key ingredients: high-quality training data, efficient training backend, and robust sandboxes.

## High-quality Training Data

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from Eigent AI’s large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates.

...

## Efficient training backend

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU's peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

...

## Robust sandbox service

During training, every attempt the agent makes runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task's environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. All of the RadixArk team's work on this release ran in sandboxes on our own service, built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, the service ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running at the same time.

Reliable as it grew. The service grew from a single machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all of them while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded, and since late October more than 99.95% have. Getting there took a steady stream of fixes and improvements, such as keeping a machine from freezing when it runs out of memory.

80% lower cost. Our cloud infrastructure cost for the project's sandboxes was about 80% lower than the cost of running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to give each sandbox memory that grows and shrinks with what it actually uses. A sandbox usually uses only a small part of the memory it asks for, so each machine can run many more sandboxes.

signals.title: SID AI Releases SID-2 Agentic Search Model With 0.720 NDCG Swarm Mode - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
November 17, 2026

SID AI has released SID-2, its second-generation agentic search model, alongside SID-2 Swarm. SID-2 is an agentic search model from SID AI that searches your data, reads results and returns ranked document IDs. It replaces fixed RAG pipelines with a model that decides what to search next. 

## TL;DR

- Size: Context window is 262k tokens per the report (256k on sid.ai/models).
- Runs on: Hosted API at platform.sid.ai, plus Baseten and SageMaker reference paths. SID’s latency figures assume 1 B200 GPU at 8 concurrent queries.
- Performance: A single agent matches Claude Opus 5.5 on retrieval quality. Swarms beat every model SID tested.
- Best: SID-2 Swarm (12 agents) scores 0.720 NDCG, above GPT-6 Astra at 0.704.
- Worst: SID-2 Low scores 0.556 NDCG, 0.148 below GPT-6 Astra. Astra still leads on California law, SEC filings and FiQA.
- Bottom line: Best: frontier-level retrieval at a fraction of the latency. Worst: no disclosed size, weights or independent evals yet.

## What is SID-2 and how does it work?

SID-2 is a small search specialist, not a general chat model. A static pipeline runs rewrite, embed, search and rerank in a fixed order. SID-2 instead searches, reads results, adapts and searches again.

Developers implement the search tools against their own backend. A `text_search` tool covers keyword search and a `search` tool covers vector search. The model ends each episode by calling `report_helpful_ids` with a ranked list. No reindexing or data movement is required, since SID-2 only sees what your tools return.

SID-2 Swarm runs several agents that message each other and fork their context into new agents. Each agent explores a separate slice of the corpus. SID argues search gains more from reading more documents than from reasoning harder about each one.

...

## How does SID-2 perform on benchmarks?

SID built a 506-question benchmark across 19 corpora. These include HotpotQA, Enron emails, SEC filings, PubMed and BrowseComp-Plus. All numbers below are self-reported from Tables 2 to 4 of the report.

- SID-2 Medium: 0.585 NDCG in 3.11 s, versus Claude Opus 5.5 (medium) at 0.577 in 25.1 s.
- SID-2 Swarm, 6 agents: 0.701 NDCG in 17.7 s, versus GPT-6 Astra (max) at 0.704 in 135 s.
- SID-2 Swarm, 12 agents: 0.720 NDCG, the highest score in the table.
- Baselines: BM25 scores 0.260 and vector search plus reranker scores 0.287.

Swarm leads on 11 of 19 corpora. On WixQA, a single high-effort agent matches Astra at about 232x lower cost. At its lowest effort, SID-2 beats 4 parallel SID-1 runs with 13x fewer FLOPs.

...

## How can developers deploy SID-2?

SID-2 is available through SID’s API and on Baseten. SDKs exist for Python (`sid-sdk`), TypeScript (`@sid-ai/sid-sdk`) and Go (`github.com/sidhq/sid-go`). A SageMaker helper covers AWS deployments. The reference implementation uses the OpenAI client format.

SID-2 costs $0.25 per million input tokens and $1.00 per million output tokens. Swarm costs $0.50 and $2.00. Cached input is 10% of the input price.

signals.excerpt:

...

- The implementation is currently an experimental project within Transformers, with the API still under discussion and no timeline for a final release.

...

Hugging Face has introduced a new approach to running large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models by streaming experts directly from SSD storage, according to a blog post published on November 18. This method allows models like the 180B parameter Qwen3.8-Flash-Next to run on hardware with limited memory, such as a 32 GB Mac, by keeping only active experts in VRAM.

The technique achieves performance within 6% of the Strata inference engine on short decode tasks, Hugging Face reported. While this offers a way to run massive models locally, the project remains an experimental implementation within Transformers, and the company noted that closing the final performance gap would require deeper changes to the current software stack.

## Technical design of expert streaming

The system works by bypassing standard offloading methods like Accelerate, which typically copy entire expert banks for every token. Instead, the new implementation switches to a streaming path where the loader skips tensors that are not immediately required. Misses are handled by eight I/O threads that perform contiguous reads for each expert, ensuring that only the routed experts cross the PCIe bus. The conversion process for these models takes approximately five hours to prepare dense weights and experts quantized to 3 bits.

To optimize performance, the system utilizes an LRU cache on the device and prebuilt Metal kernels. The engine improves prefill speeds by "reading the next layer's experts while the current layer is being computed," Hugging Face noted. The project also incorporates quantized weights, specifically using 3-bit experts and 8-bit dense layers, to reduce the memory footprint during execution. This allows the model to use approximately 18 GiB after loading, with a 6K prompt peaking at 25.4 GiB.

## Comparison with existing inference engines

Hugging Face evaluated this streaming approach against established engines including llama.cpp and vLLM. While llama.cpp uses mmap to keep experts on the CPU, it can fragment the graph, leading to performance losses. Similarly, vLLM's offloading strategies often involve high overhead, as hot experts may cross the PCIe bus repeatedly without effective caching. In tests on an A10G GPU with 24 GB of memory, offloading only the experts doubled vLLM's speed, while using FP8 helped keep more of the model on the GPU.

Inference engine performance comparison

This table compares the decode speed in tokens per second across various inference engines and configurations.

Inference engine performance comparison

| Engine | Decode (tok/s) |
| --- | --- |
| Strata, Q8_0 | 82 - 88 |
| llama.cpp, Q8_0, --fit on | 63 - 64 |
| llama.cpp, BF16, --fit on | 35 - 36 |
| vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts | 20.1 |
| vLLM, FP8, same flags, --enforce-eager | 14.7 |
| vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 | 9.7 |
| vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts | 7.3 |
| vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 | 3.3 |
| Transformers + Accelerate | 0.16 |

Method: Reproduced from the table published by Hugging Face. Source: Hugging Face: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers, retrieved 19 Nov 2026

The new Transformers-based implementation aims to bridge the gap between these engines and the specialized Strata engine.

...

The developer noted that while the system runs at approximately 14 tokens per second, it remains slower than desired for specific coding agent workflows. Future progress depends on gaining deeper control over per-layer synchronization, a capability that is currently restricted by the underlying PyTorch framework. The project serves as a systems-level exploration of how sparse routing and expert caching impact LLM performance, providing insights into where memory bandwidth is consumed per token.

The API for this streaming implementation is currently being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The developer emphasized that closing the final performance gap would require deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over per-layer synchronization, which is not currently available.

signals.title: Korea's AI Firms Turn to Inference Tuning to Cut Soaring GPU Costs - Seoul Economic Daily
signals.excerpt:
Published 2026.11.18. 17:45:31

...

Cutting and Compressing to Make Models Lighter

Lightweighting is the leading method of making AI models more efficient. The approach reduces the memory a model occupies and the volume of computation it requires, allowing the model to run on fewer computing resources.

Lightweighting is drawing attention because the cost burden grows as demand for AI inference rises. "Inference occurs every time a user accesses a service, so the computing resources and costs required rise along with the number of users," said Kim Hyung-jun, CEO of SqueezeBits. "For services with large models, such as generative AI, or heavy computation, such as image and video generation, how efficiently the model runs directly affects service costs and speed."

The center of gravity in AI computing is also shifting from training to inference, adding to the need for lightweighting. According to global accounting and consulting firm Deloitte, inference accounted for just one-third of all AI computing three years ago but is expected to reach two-thirds this year, surpassing training. The change reflects growing demand to use AI in actual work rather than merely develop it.

The lightweighting techniques most widely used in the industry include pruning, quantization and graph optimization. Pruning works by cutting away less important connections and components among a model's many neural networks, much like trimming small branches so a tree grows better.

Quantization compresses data represented in 32 bits down to 8-bit or 4-bit units. Graph optimization, another leading technique, reduces how often data moves to high-bandwidth memory during computation and rearranges the order of operations so they can be processed faster. "Graph optimization does not degrade the quality of computational results, while quantization and pruning affect quality to some degree," said Yoo Seung-joo, a professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at Seoul National University. "Quality may decline slightly, but what matters is staying within a reasonable line so the difference is not noticeable."

GPUs Running at Only 30% Are Also Targets for Optimization

Shrinking a model does not automatically make it faster or cheaper. The hardware running the lighter model, such as graphics processing units, must be able to handle the altered computation method efficiently. That is why techniques for making models lighter must be paired with optimization that draws out maximum hardware performance. "Each piece of hardware handles different operations well and supports different data formats, and memory structures and data movement methods also differ," Kim said. "Even with the same GPU, the optimal settings can change when the product or generation changes."

GPU efficiency is also considered an important element in cutting AI inference costs. Prices run from tens of millions of won to more than 100 million won per card, and the chips are hard to obtain. Demand to use hard-won GPUs as efficiently as possible is inevitably high. "You basically cannot run a GPU at 100%, and only 30% to 50% is used for effective computation," said Kim Joon-gi, chief technology officer at Lablup. "GPU computation halts while data is sent and received over the network or read and written, and making that more efficient has recently become a major interest in the industry."

Nvidia's MIG and MPS methods are cited as technologies that let a single GPU be divided across multiple tasks. MIG partitions one GPU at the hardware level, much like dividing a single office into several rooms where work is carried out separately. Its defining feature is stable GPU use without interference from other users or tasks. Unlike MIG, MPS allows multiple programs to share a GPU simultaneously at the software level. It resembles several people doing different tasks in one office: the GPU can be divided according to usage, but if one task stops working, the entire GPU can come to a halt. "Depending on the type and characteristics of the tasks running simultaneously on a GPU, overall computing speed can fall by less than 5%," the CTO said. "But total throughput rises, so productivity improves."

...

Many companies are already making the most of these technologies to improve AI and GPU efficiency. Upstage applied Nota's AI model lightweighting technology to its recently released Solar Open2 model. As a result, work that previously required eight Nvidia H100 GPUs can now be handled with two. Nota also applied its lightweighting technology to Alibaba's AI model Qwen 3.8 Max, cutting the number of B300 GPUs needed from 24 to four. SqueezeBits applied its technology to Nvidia's world model Cosmos and achieved inference speeds about 3.1 times faster. At Lablup, a client that used the company's GPU resource management optimization solution saw GPU utilization rise to 85% from 35%.

Efficiency work is growing more complex, however, as AI models diversify from large language models into video and speech recognition models. "With LLMs, you have to check whether accuracy of answers and the ability to follow instructions hold up on core tasks, and with video recognition models, you have to examine whether specific objects are missed in footage," Kim said. "If necessary, performance has to be supplemented through additional training."

signals.title: Stripe launches evals to benchmark how well coding agents build payment integrations
signals.excerpt:
Stripe has released a public benchmark that grades AI coding agents on one specific job: building Stripe integrations that actually work.

The project, called Stripe evals, launched publicly on November 19, 2026. The headline finding is humbling for the machines. Agents averaged roughly 78% of the required criteria, but only 29% of runs fully met all of them.

## What Stripe is actually measuring

The benchmark spans 11 reproducible environments split into three buckets. The first covers backend-only tasks. The second covers full-stack workflows, where results are checked in a real browser. The third bucket is a set of specialized “gym” problem sets. These zero in on specific Stripe features, including Checkout and subscription billing.

Stripe compares performance across three variables: the harness, the model, and the integration scenario. A harness is the scaffolding that wraps a model and gives it tools.

The company says it plans to publish fresh results periodically. The stated goal is to help businesses pick the agent configuration that best fits their needs.

## The tooling and the scoreboard

Under the hood, the framework runs on a Goose-based agent harness. It pairs that with Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, which let agents reach outside the chat window.

Through MCP, agents get terminal access, browser automation, and documentation lookup.

The most interesting number may belong to Stripe’s own plugin. Across the tested model and harness combinations, it lifted scores by 3 to 8 percentage points. It also cut the need for web searches by 96%. Extraneous test code fell by approximately 40%.

On the model leaderboard, Claude Opus 4.5 posted a 92% average on full-stack tasks. GPT-5.2 reached 73% on the gym sets, using a best-of-three approach.

The tasks were not trivial, either. Agents averaged 63 turns in their best runs, meaning dozens of back-and-forth steps to finish a single integration.

...

The caveat is that any benchmark measures what it measures. Eleven environments cover a lot of ground, but they cannot capture every company’s quirks, legacy systems, or unusual pricing models.

signals.excerpt:
###### The Linux Foundation | 19 November 2026

Distributed KV Caching Maximizes GPU Servers and Minimizes Costs

Agentic AI applications waste expensive GPU compute by constantly reprocessing the same prompt instructions, tool definitions, and conversation history. Released alongside Valkey 9.2, open source distributed KV caching enhances AI workload efficiency by creating a large, shared cache across a GPU fleet, allowing inference engines to reuse computed work rather than recomputing. Builders running open-weight models on self-managed inference can now connect a distributed KV cache through LMCache, which plugs into engines like vLLM and SGLang using a single configuration change. Distributed KV caching achieves:

- Lower AI inference spend: Reduces costs by up to 40% by allowing teams to serve more users on the GPUs they already have.
- Improved latency: Decreases time-to-first-token by up to 80%.
- Seamless deployment, no vendor-lock in: Works on any cloud or infrastructure with zero application code updates.

## Path Hash Makes Finding AI Context More Efficient

While distributed KV caching saves expensive compute, efficiently locating that shared context has traditionally required engineering teams to build and maintain complex, custom lookup logic. Valkey 9.2 minimizes this burden with Path Hash, a new native data type that acts as a fast, lightweight index for AI caching.
